name: RISC-V

claims.claim_text: RISC-V is an instruction set architecture rather than a processor: a from-scratch design that conforms to it is still entirely your own silicon, and what conformance buys is that an existing compiler can target it.
claims.quote_verbatim: is an instruction set architecture. It's not a processor. So if you design a processor from scratch, it would be compliant with the instruction set architecture, which means you'd have a decent chance of having a compiler being able to write code for your target
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: An open ISA carries no guarantee that any implementation is open; a core described as RISC-V may be entirely proprietary, and the extensions it carries are equally unconstrained, so an open CPU has to be verified as a separate claim.
claims.quote_verbatim: with RISC-V, you have that instruction set architecture that's open, but the implementations are, there's no guarantee whatsoever or extensions
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: The licence does not flow down from the instruction set to the implementation: a company can take the ISA, design a core, and sell that core as proprietary soft IP or as hard silicon without publishing anything.
claims.quote_verbatim: do you have to make all of that open as well nope no you don't
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Standardisation stops at the instruction set. Nothing outside the core is specified, which is why groups of vendors have to form separate consortia to agree reference architectures for interoperable parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: the core is like the instruction set is standardized, but outside of that, nothing else is standardized
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The base integer instruction set is roughly 47 instructions, with custom extensions layered on top; the small mandatory core is what makes a compliant implementation tractable for one person.
claims.quote_verbatim: the risk 5 base is small contains just 47 instructions
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A working RISC-V core has been published in on the order of a hundred lines of Verilog and fits in about 1380 logic units on a small Lattice iCE40 part, running a real blinky demonstration.
claims.quote_verbatim: he uses 1380 logic units
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A compiler is not finished when it targets your processor: it needs a large user base inspecting generated code closely enough to write and contribute test cases, which a one-off private ISA never accumulates.
claims.quote_verbatim: need also a lot of people using that compiler and looking at the compiler output very, very closely
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: The economic argument for a shared ISA is that the ecosystem work is done once and reused by every subsequent processor, instead of being redone from scratch each time someone builds a new core.
claims.quote_verbatim: with risk five, the idea is we only need to do that once
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: Before a common open ISA existed, a free core was typically either legally encumbered — usable until the product got big enough to attract the IP holder's attention — or a one-person design whose GCC fork was never mainlined and had not been updated in years, leaving something antique like a Z80 or 8051 as the safe option.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would have a few CPU cores that were really nice, but they were made by one random guy who also developed the ISA and there is a GCC
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg

claims.claim_text: What the shared ISA changed in practice is that cores of wildly different sizes can be dropped into a design and all of them share one actively maintained, stable compiler.
claims.quote_verbatim: can just go and download the RISC-V GCC thing, which is actively being developed on by a lot of people, which is stable
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg

claims.claim_text: Designing a custom processor against a common ISA removes the obligation to also build the language, the opcodes and the operating-system support; the translation layer already exists, which is what makes the exercise finishable.
claims.quote_verbatim: because of the common ISA, it's like, okay, I don't have to write
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Because GCC absorbed the instruction set and its compilation down to those instructions is tested, retargeting a build to RISC-V is close to a compiler flag change rather than a port — the same property that would apply to any other ISA the compiler supports.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could just switch a flag in gcc and it starts targeting risk five
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: x86 is fast because of the processors built around it, not because of its instruction set; a large fraction of the die area goes into instruction decode, which is exactly the overhead a reduced instruction set avoids and why embedded parts went that way.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the area in an x86 processor is actually dedicated to things like decoding instructions
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: Comparing one instruction set against another on performance is a category error; only implementations can be compared, and nothing in a clean modern ISA prevents building a high-performance processor from it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only thing that really makes sense is compare implementations with implementations
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: A 32-bit RISC soft core fits in roughly half of a 5,000 logic-element FPGA, leaving the other half for custom peripherals — which sets the practical floor for what device you need to host a soft processor plus your own logic.
claims.quote_verbatim: has a fairly small FPGA, about 5,000 logic elements. But nevertheless, if you want to build a 32-bit processor for it, it maybe takes up half of the space
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: A well-optimised open core such as VexRiscv puts a multi-core Linux-capable SoC into an FPGA of about 35,000 LUTs or fewer, rather than requiring a large high-end device.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can put a multi-core Linux capable SOC into your FPGA
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: The same soft RISC-V core moved from an older 40 nm low-power FPGA family to a newer process went from about 100 MHz to about 400 MHz, a jump large enough that customers assumed a measurement error.
claims.quote_verbatim: run my RISV processor on try on it's only 100 megahertz it's 400 megahertz now
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: Once a soft core clocks at 400 to 500 MHz on the fabric, adding a hardwired processor subsystem to the die stops paying for itself — the logic area is better spent on more fabric, and the soft core is offered instead as a modifiable SoC template.
claims.quote_verbatim: if someone optimizes well you can run processor at 400-500 megahertz so you don't necessarily build a hard wire system
claims.speaker: Sammy Cheung

claims.claim_text: Custom instruction-set extensions are open to anyone, and on a part that also carries embedded FPGA fabric those custom instructions can be implemented in the fabric, turning an extension into a hardware accelerator for operations such as convolution.
claims.quote_verbatim: anybody can sort of come out with their own extension to the instruction set
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: A soft core lets you rearrange the hardware to suit the software: gathering eight bits that live in eight different registers into one register turns roughly sixteen instructions of reads and XORs into a single read, an eight-fold speedup that makes a 20 MHz soft processor behave far better than its clock suggests.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you need to read eight, you know, bits from eight different registers, you could rearrange that. So it's only one read
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Moving a function from software into dedicated hardware is often what removes the need for a fast processor at all, which reframes a slow soft core as a design starting point rather than a limitation.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you move something from software into hardware, it can get significantly more efficient. Maybe you don't need that gigahertz CPU
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Sub-word writes on the 32-bit bus are signalled rather than masked: the core always drives a full 32-bit value and uses the write strobes to say which bytes are meant, so a peripheral that ignores the strobes will corrupt neighbouring bytes.
claims.quote_verbatim: it'll send a 32-bit value over, but it'll tell you using the right strobe, oh, I only want to write this byte of the 32-bit value
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg

claims.claim_text: The CH32V debug interface avoids a complex protocol entirely: it exposes a small scratchpad, you write RISC-V code into it, and a command halts the running program and executes that code on the core — so flashing and memory access are just short programs rather than protocol commands.
claims.quote_verbatim: it gives you access to this, this little scratch pad where you can write code into the scratch pad
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Dual-architecture boot is handled in the binary header: the mask ROM reads a flag saying whether the image is an ARM or a RISC-V binary and reboots the chip into the matching set of cores, so the architecture is chosen by the program rather than by a fuse or a part number.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's just a flag in there saying if it's an ARM or a RISC-V binary
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: The RISC-V cores added to a mainstream microcontroller were small enough to fit the existing socket without growing the die, and were justified mainly as an education vehicle — both for users and for the design team learning to implement a new architecture in a conventional system.
claims.quote_verbatim: they are small enough that you can kind of sneak them in without increasing the die size
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A draft debug specification is a blocking defect for a product design freeze: the debug spec is not just JTAG but new control and status registers and an entire privileged mode, so core semantics were still subject to change while the chip had to be committed.
claims.quote_verbatim: the debug specification for risk five was still in draft status
claims.speaker: Luke Renn
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Debug capability is the deciding criterion in embedded architecture selection because there is no other way to see inside the running system, which is enough on its own to send a design to a mature architecture even when the engineer prefers the alternative.
claims.quote_verbatim: debug really is everything in embedded because you can't see inside the system any other way
claims.speaker: Luke Renn
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: A verified management core placed alongside the user area of a shared-shuttle chip turns bring-up into software: it boots reliably, exposes virtual GPIO into the user design, and can enable, disable and probe blocks that may themselves be broken.
claims.quote_verbatim: it can be used to probe other parts of the chip and turn on and off other parts of the chip as a piece of software
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Pin count, not silicon area, is the binding constraint when several processors share a die; the answer is multiplexers on the IO so a user can select which design reaches the outside world.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have enough pins to effectively have, um, you know, each risk five have its own dedicated set of pins
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Without a RAM compiler available, memory on an early open-source SoC had to be built out of logic cells; the later revision keeps identical content but swaps in compiled RAM, and the difference is visible on the die as a block rather than a spread of logic.
claims.quote_verbatim: we didn't have the compiler ready, the RAM compiler
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: The first microcontroller built from a RISC-V core with a fully open-source tool set was assembled by splitting the work — an outside CPU author, a party with foundry access and analog IP, and a system integrator — and its value was demonstrating feasibility on real silicon rather than competitive performance.
claims.quote_verbatim: a microcontroller based on a risk five CPU with a hundred percent open source tool set
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Guaranteeing that one known processor is always present in a modular chiplet system gives the software a fixed base to boot from, so the variable parts can then be discovered and configured automatically at runtime.
claims.quote_verbatim: we made our life a little bit easier by always having a risk five processor running there
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Describing hardware in a full programming language rather than plain Verilog lets a core be generated from parameters — memory management unit, floating point, vector support — so one project emits a different CPU per configuration instead of shipping one fixed design.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can turn on and off all these different parameters. Do you want a memory management unit? Do you want floating point? Do you want vector? And it generates a whole different CPU
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Ibex is the RISC-V core developed by lowRISC and also used in OpenTitan; CHERI is a separate set of extensions layered on it that add memory compartmentalisation, so the two names describe different layers of the same board.
claims.quote_verbatim: is this risk risk five core that low risk developed
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Tool chain maturity dominates architecture selection: the chains for established parts are well proven and long-lived, and engineers who have to ship a product are rationally conservative about working with unknown tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: have to worry about the tool chains
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Mainstream microcontrollers and their heavily used compilers still surface bugs, so an architecture with a small user base should be assumed to hide proportionally more undiscovered problems — a real risk to weigh when starting a product on one.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've had enough issues with, you know, mainstream processes, you know, the ST ones in the compilers that like everyone's using. And yet we still run into issues
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: For a commercial SoC the incumbent architecture wins on availability, verification, documentation and the existence of genuinely high-performance cores; the maturity gap runs x86 first, ARM second and RISC-V some distance behind, and software tooling maturity follows the same order.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's very easy to get hold of ARM IP. It works very well. It's well tested. It's well documented
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: Competitive pressure from the open ISA improved terms on the incumbent: the licensing processes for getting hold of ARM IP became easier, which benefits designers who never intend to switch architectures.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've made ARM a bit keener and they've changed some of their processes to make getting their IP a bit easier
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: A large microcontroller vendor's customers decline RISC-V parts on ecosystem grounds, so the vendor deploys the architecture where it is invisible to the customer — inside an FPGA or a data-centre part — rather than as the advertised core.
claims.quote_verbatim: wouldn't take the, you know, risk-based part today because they don't believe there is enough ecosystem
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: Cores are the abundant part and the least valuable: a CPU is not usable without GPIO drivers, programmable IO, PWM, converters, timers and interrupts, which is the forty-peripheral surround that a mature vendor microcontroller supplies and a bare core does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: already so many risk five CPU cores. So, but they're not, they're not really much good on their own. They need GPIO drivers
claims.speaker: Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Building your own processor when a commodity one would do misreads what the open ISA enables; it opens a different application space rather than replacing the case for buying an off-the-shelf part.
claims.quote_verbatim: why wouldn't you go buy that Toyota Corolla or that ARM processor
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: A published teardown analysis of the ten-cent RISC-V microcontroller concluded it is not the best cheap part available — a comparable 48 MHz Cortex-M0 from a memory manufacturer meets the same brief — so the architecture itself, not measured advantage, is much of what draws interest to it.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is actually not the best chip you can get for cheap
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Fluency in ARM, x86 and AVR assembly does not transfer cleanly: an engineer with all three found working in RISC-V assembly a genuine struggle, so hand-written low-level work on a new architecture should be budgeted as a learning cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: know ARM assembly pretty well. I know extensive assembly better. And I know x86 assembly better than that
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: MounRiver is the vendor's proprietary Eclipse-based development environment for the CH32V line, where CH marks the Chinese semiconductor maker WCH and the V marks RISC-V.
claims.quote_verbatim: River is the proprietary sort of development kit environment for the CH32V003
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For a fabless analog startup, putting a RISC-V style processor next to the analog section removes an ARM licensing negotiation from the schedule, which is one of several factors that make small chip companies viable again — the harder questions remain whether the niche is real and how the work is funded.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could make a, a case for even adding on risk five style processors along
claims.speaker: Anthony Wall
claims.episode_title: ADC Chip Design with Anthony Wall

claims.claim_text: During the worst of the shortage, designing a custom SoC and having it fabricated would have been faster than waiting out lead times on a commodity microcontroller — an inversion that says more about supply conditions than about design effort.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a time when we were, would have been quicker to have designed your own RISC-V SOC and had it fabricated than wait for some STM32s
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: Embedded controllers hidden in commodity parts have historically been idiosyncratic — SD cards found running an 8051 with 32-bit extensions — and are poor things to expose to large numbers of end users; a common ISA with rapidly improving GCC, Clang and LLVM support is a better target for anything meant to be programmed.
claims.quote_verbatim: found those SD cards were using like an 8051 with 32-bit extensions
claims.speaker: David Shah

claims.claim_text: MIPS, the architecture famously chosen over ARM for the PIC32 line, announced that its next-generation architecture would be based on RISC-V rather than developed further on its own instruction set.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're developing a new industry leading standards, eighth generation architecture, which we will be basing on the open source risk five processor standard
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Architecture selection is not a referendum on architecture quality: the engineer who rejected RISC-V for a product held it in high regard and had implementations of his own, and the decision turned on one unfinished specification.
claims.quote_verbatim: risk five is a brilliant architecture. It's a really beautiful piece of engineering
claims.speaker: Luke Renn
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

attribution_notes: attribution_reliable was not trusted. ep374 labels every turn 'Claire Wolf' including the host's questions; the technical answers about compilers, ISA design and formal verification are attributed to Claire Wolf by content, and the interviewer's turns were not used.
ep519 (Michael Gielda) and ep651 (Jeff Geerling) carry the same all-one-speaker pattern; only material unambiguously belonging to the guest was used.
ep637 labels the guest's remarks about assembly-language fluency as 'Chris Gammell', but the host addresses the guest by name immediately afterwards; that claim is attributed to CNLohr by content.
ep529 and ep648 both feature the Raspberry Pi team; claims are attributed to the named engineer whose first-person account the passage records.
One passage in the bundle carries episode: null and was dropped as uncitable.

The bundle is dominated by market commentary — who is jumping on which bandwagon, whether the growth is surprising, whether ARM is nervous. All of that was excluded as reception and speculation; only design-relevant constraints, numbers, procedures and anchored judgments were kept.
